segments.english: Come, let us make our father drink wine, and let us lie with him, and let us preserve offspring from our father.
segments.literal: come, let-us-make-drink (object marker) our-father wine, and-let-us-lie with-him, and-let-us-keep-alive from-our-father seed

tokens.note: Imperative of הָלַךְ with the paragogic ה. Radak takes לְכָה as an interjection of agreement, like לְכוּ and הָבָה: it opens a joint proposal rather than sending anyone anywhere.
Hifil of שָׁקָה, the causative of drinking. The form is a yiqtol in the first common plural, read here as a proposal ('let us').
The object marker אֵת, not the preposition: it marks אָבִינוּ as the one who drinks.
Cohortative of שָׁכַב. With עִם the verb means to lie with, that is, to have intercourse.
Piel of חָיָה: to preserve alive, keep alive. The seed is the object.
מִן marks the source: the seed would come through the father.
זֶרַע here is offspring, the line that carries on.

phrases.literal: 'come': the interjection that opens the proposal (Radak)

phrases.english: let us make our father drink wine
phrases.literal: 'let-us-make-drink (object marker) our-father wine': the causative hifil; the object marker is not translated

phrases.english: and let us lie with him
phrases.literal: 'and-let-us-lie with-him': the second act of the proposal

phrases.english: and let us preserve offspring from our father
phrases.literal: 'and-let-us-keep-alive from-our-father seed': the piel 'preserve alive' takes seed (offspring) as its object; 'from our father' is the source

grammar: לְכָה is the one word of address in the verse. It is singular and masculine, but Radak notes that such interjections do not vary for number or gender, since they express agreement.
The three verbs that follow are all first common plural: נַשְׁקֶה, וְנִשְׁכְּבָה, וּנְחַיֶּה. Each one is a step in the proposal, and the English 'let us' carries them all.
The verb נַשְׁקֶה is a yiqtol in form, a causative (hifil) of שָׁקָה. The English 'make ... drink' keeps the causative and the object.
The second and third steps are joined to the first by ו (and). The English keeps 'and' only where the Hebrew has the conjunction on the verb.

commentary.summary: Radak: לָכָה, like לְכוּ and הָבָה, expresses agreement and mutual help ('let us'), and does not vary for gender or number. The English 'Come' with 'let us' keeps the sense of a proposal made to companions.
Radak gives the purpose of the drinking: until the father is drunk and does not know what he does. The English line states the act and leaves its purpose to the reader.

Ramban: perhaps they reasoned that they should do what was fitting, that God would have mercy, and that a male and a female would be born and the world would continue through them ('the world is built by kindness', Ps 89:3), since the LORD had not saved them for nothing. They were modest and did not tell their father to take them, because a descendant of Noah may marry his daughter, or because the thing was very ugly in the eyes of those generations and had never been done; and our rabbis in the aggadot condemn Lot severely. This is the motive the daughters may have had; it is not a gloss on any word, so the English gives none.

Radak: one who leaves no seed is as dead, if he leaves nothing after him by which his name is remembered. This gives the daughters' reason for wanting offspring; it does not bear on the wording of the English.

context: In the world of the text a family line continues through children, above all sons, and the name of a dead man is kept alive by his descendants. To be left without offspring was to be cut off; many stories in Genesis turn on this. The daughters give exactly this aim: to preserve offspring from their father.

segments.english: And they made their father drink wine that night, and the firstborn came in and lay with her father, and he did not perceive when she lay down and when she rose.
segments.literal: and-they-made-drink (object marker) their-father wine in-the-night that, and-came-in the-firstborn and-lay with(אֵת) her-father, and-not he-perceived in-her-lying-down and-in-her-rising

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of the hifil, feminine plural: the two daughters are the subject.

The article is on the noun (הַלַּיְלָה, with the ב: 'in the night'). The demonstrative הוּא 'that' follows without its own article, though the article is expected (הַהוּא, as in 19:35). Radak calls this the lack of the ה of the definite article on the adjective and compares 2 Sam 6:3 and Num 28:4.
Wayyiqtol of בּוֹא, 'go in, come in'; the same verb is used of a man going in to a woman. The verse does not name the place.
Wayyiqtol of שָׁכַב, the sexual sense, with the preposition אֵת that follows.
Here אֵת is the preposition 'with' (together with), not the object marker; the same idiom as the verb 'lie with'.
The negation covers both infinitives that follow.
The father did not notice her lying down or her rising. Radak notes that if he had perceived her rising he would have quarrelled with them.

Infinitive construct with ב and a 3rd feminine singular suffix: 'in her lying down'. Ibn Ezra: it is the infinitive (שֵׁם הַפּוֹעַל), though its first vowel is hireq (שִׁכְבָהּ), as in בְּשִׁבְרִי לָכֶם (Lev 26:26). The plain 'lying down' is the act with her father in the context.
Infinitive construct with ו and ב: 'and in her rising'. The ו carries a puncta extraordinaria in the Masoretic text (see apparatus).

phrases.english: And they made their father drink wine
phrases.literal: 'and-they-made-drink (object marker) their-father wine': the wayyiqtol opens the narrative; the object marker is not translated
'in-the-night that': the night with its demonstrative
'and-came-in the-firstborn': the verb comes before the subject
'and-lay with (object marker) her-father': the preposition אֵת, 'with', as in 'lay with'
'and-not he-perceived': the negation governs both infinitives after it
'in-her-lying-down': the infinitive with ב
'and-in-her-rising': the second infinitive, with ו

grammar: The narrative is in the wayyiqtol throughout (וַתַּשְׁקֶין, וַתָּבֹא, וַתִּשְׁכַּב): the sequence of past events.
The verb of perception is the qatal יָדַע, negated, and the two infinitives that follow are what he did not notice. The sentence says the father did not notice either act.
The verb שָׁכַב takes אֵת here and עִם in 19:35. The English uses 'lay with' for both, so the difference of preposition is kept in the literal line.
The infinitives בְּשִׁכְבָהּ and וּבְקוּמָהּ are a fixed pair: the first is the lying down, the second the rising, and the verse denies notice of both.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: בְּשִׁכְבָהּ is the infinitive (שֵׁם הַפּוֹעַל), even though its first letter has a hireq, like בְּשִׁבְרִי לָכֶם (Lev 26:26). The English reads it as the event: 'when she lay down'.
Radak: the demonstrative הוּא stands after the noun without the article, so הַלַּיְלָה הוּא means 'that night'. The English keeps 'that night'.

Radak: 'he did not perceive' covers even her rising, because of his drunkenness; the verse says it so that the reader knows that a waking father would have quarrelled. The English keeps the negation over both acts.

Rashi: of the younger it is written 'and she lay with him' (not 'with her father'); because she did not begin the immorality but her sister taught her, scripture spared her and did not spell out her shame, whereas the firstborn, who began it, scripture exposes explicitly ('with her father'). A moral reading of the wording; the English renders both acts alike.

Rashi: the puncta on the ו of בּוּקוּמָהּ show that the father knew at her rising, though he did not guard himself the second night. The English declines this: the verb's negation governs both infinitives, as Radak's plain reading also takes it, and the pointing is a midrashic reading, not the plain sense.
Radak's note on the dotted ו gives the midrashic reading that the father knew at her rising. The English does not adopt it, for the reason given at rashi:19:33:3.

apparatus: The ו of וּבְקוּמָהּ carries a puncta extraordinaria in the Masoretic text (the WLC note in the pack). Rashi and Radak cite the midrash that the point means he knew at her rising; the English declines it.

segments.english: On the next day the firstborn said to the younger, "Look, I lay with my father last night. Let us make him drink wine tonight also, and go in and lie with him, and let us preserve offspring from our father."
segments.literal: and-it-came-to-pass from-the-morrow and-said the-firstborn to the-younger: look, I-lay last-night with(אֵת) my-father; let-us-make-drink-him wine also the-night, and-go-in (f.) lie (f.) with-him, and-let-us-keep-alive from-our-father seed

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of הָיָה with a temporal phrase: 'and it came to pass'. A standard narrative opener.
מָחֳרָת, the morrow: the day after the night of 19:33.
צָעִיר, adjective in the feminine: 'the younger one'. Its entry gives no sense beyond 'young'.
הֵן, the particle that draws attention in speech. Rendered 'look', not 'behold'.
Qatal, first common singular: a completed act, reported by the elder.
אֶמֶשׁ: the night just past. Radak: the night that has passed is called emesh.
The preposition אֵת, 'with' (together with), not the object marker.
Cohortative hifil with a 3rd masculine singular suffix: 'let us make him drink'.
גַּם: 'also', joining tonight to the night before.
הַלַּיְלָה: the coming night.
Imperative feminine singular: addressed to the younger alone.
Imperative feminine singular of שָׁכַב, the sexual sense.

phrases.literal: 'and-it-came-to-pass from-the-morrow': the wayyiqtol as a time opener
'and-said the-firstborn': the subject follows the verb
'to the-younger'

phrases.english: Look, I lay with my father last night
phrases.literal: 'look I-lay last-night with(אֵת) my-father': the speech opens; the perfect states the completed act

phrases.english: Let us make him drink wine tonight also
phrases.literal: 'let-us-make-drink-him wine also the-night': the cohortative proposes the same act for the coming night
'and-go-in': the imperative, addressed to the younger
'lie with-him': the imperative of שָׁכַב with עִם

phrases.english: and let us preserve offspring from our father
phrases.literal: 'and-let-us-keep-alive from-our-father seed': the piel as in 19:32

grammar: The speech changes person: the elder speaks of her completed act in the first singular (שָׁכַבְתִּי), then proposes in the first plural (נַשְׁקֶנּוּ, וּנְחַיֶּה), and gives the younger her part in the second feminine singular (וּבֹאִי, שִׁכְבִי).

נַשְׁקֶנּוּ is the hifil cohortative with the suffix 'him' joined by a doubled nun (an energic ending): 'let us make him drink'. The clause repeats the act of 19:33 for the next night: 'also tonight' is the English of גַּם הַלַּיְלָה.
The reported act of the elder is in the qatal, and she gives its time as אֶמֶשׁ, the night just past.
The speech ends with the same clause as the elder's proposal in 19:32 (וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע), now spoken to the younger as the reason for the second night.

commentary.summary: Radak: the night just passed is called אֶמֶשׁ. The English 'last night' gives this sense.

segments.english: And they made their father drink wine also that night, and the younger arose and lay with him, and he did not perceive when she lay down and when she rose.
segments.literal: and-they-made-drink also in-the-night that (object marker) their-father wine, and-arose the-younger and-lay with-him, and-not he-perceived in-her-lying-down and-in-her-rising

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of the hifil, feminine plural, as in 19:33.1.
גַּם: the second night is set beside the first.
Wayyiqtol of קוּם. 'Arose' begins the action: she got up and lay with him. The verb is the ordinary one for getting up and also opens a sequence of acts.
Wayyiqtol of שָׁכַב, the sexual sense.
The younger uses עִם; the firstborn in 19:33 used אֵת.
The negation covers both infinitives.
Infinitive construct with ב and a 3rd feminine singular suffix.

Infinitive construct with ו and ב: 'and in her rising'. Here the word is written without the ו after the ק (קֻמָהּ, with qibbuts); in 19:33 it is קוּמָהּ with the extra dots. Radak: it is written defectively, without a vav. The verb is the same.

phrases.english: And they made their father drink wine also that night
phrases.literal: 'and-they-made-drink also in-the-night that (object marker) their-father wine': the object marker is not translated
'and-arose the-younger': the verb comes before the subject
'and-lay with-him': the sexual sense with עִם
'and-not he-perceived': the negation governs both infinitives
'in-her-lying-down': the infinitive with ב
'and-in-her-rising': the second infinitive

grammar: The verse repeats the frame of 19:33 with these changes: the subject (the younger), the verb of motion (וַתָּקׇם 'arose' for וַתָּבֹא 'came in'), the preposition (עִם for אֵת), the adverb גַּם 'also', the fuller הַהוּא 'that' (19:33 has הוּא), and the defective spelling בְּקֻמָהּ.

In both nights it is the daughters (plural) who make the father drink (19:33, 19:35); only the act of lying with him is done by one daughter each night, the elder first and then the younger. The father's ignorance is the same in both.
The adverb גַּם ties the second night to the first, as the speech in 19:34 had done.

commentary.summary: Radak: the word וּבְקֻמָהּ is written defectively, without a vav (unlike וּבְקוּמָהּ in 19:33). A remark on the spelling; it does not change the English.

segments.english: And the two daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father.

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of הָרָה, feminine plural: the two daughters are the subject. The text gives no separate date for the conception.
The feminine dual form שְׁתֵּי in the construct: 'two daughters'.
מִן marks the father as the source, as 'from' in 19:32.9; the English gives it as 'by'.

phrases.english: And the two daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father
phrases.literal: 'and-they-became-pregnant the-two-of daughters-of Lot from-their-father': the verb first, then the subject and the source

grammar: The verb is a wayyiqtol of הָרָה in the feminine plural, with the two daughters as subject; the English 'became pregnant' is the sense of the verb's Qal 1 entry.
The construct phrase שְׁתֵּי בְנוֹת־לוֹט is 'the two daughters of Lot': a construct chain ending in a proper name is definite, so the whole phrase has the sense of the article.
The verse gives the conception without a separate night for each daughter: the reader is left to place it.

commentary.summary: Rashi: although a woman does not conceive from a first act of intercourse, these two took control of themselves and put their nakedness (their private parts) outward, and so conceived from the first act. The English does not adopt this physiological explanation; it is kept here because a reader may ask how both conceived after one night each.

Radak: they conceived from that one act, which shows that they did not lie with him again, for their only aim was to leave seed. The English 'became pregnant', set after each daughter's one night, agrees.

segments.english: The firstborn bore a son and named him Moab; he is the father of the Moabites to this day.
segments.literal: and-bore the-firstborn son and-named his-name Moab; he father-of Moab to the-day

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of יָלַד, the woman's bearing.
Wayyiqtol of קָרָא, 'call, name'.
The name is the object of the naming: 'called his name Moab', rendered as 'named him Moab'.

tokens.gloss: Moab ('from the father', as the text plays on it)
tokens.note: The name is a transliteration. The text gives the name by sound-play on מֵאָב, 'from a father' (compare מֵאֲבִיהֶן, 19:36). Ibn Ezra: 'like מֵאָב'. Radak: 'from a father I had this son'. The English keeps the name, as the decisions require.
The pronoun resumes the son as subject of the nominal clause.
אָב in the sense of the founder of a people, the 'father of his people'.
Moab as the nation descended from the son.

phrases.literal: 'bore the-firstborn son': the verb first, then the subject
'and-named his-name Moab': the idiom 'named him' for 'called his name'

phrases.english: he is the father of the Moabites
phrases.literal: 'he father-of Moab': a nominal clause, with 'is' implicit in the Hebrew
'to the-day': the fixed phrase עַד הַיּוֹם

grammar: The verse has two parts: the naming (wayyiqtol forms) and a nominal clause with a resumptive pronoun (הוּא אֲבִי מוֹאָב).
The name מוֹאָב is given as the son's name and then as the name of the people; the English uses 'Moab' for the son and 'the Moabites' for the people.
The final phrase עַד הַיּוֹם is a fixed idiom: 'to this day', a reference to the time of the telling.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: מוֹאָב is 'like' מֵאָב, 'from a father': the name is the sound-play of the daughter's words. The gloss and the note give this; the English line keeps the name, as the decisions require.

Rashi: the firstborn named her son with the explicit 'from my father', and the younger named hers in clean language, and was rewarded in the days of Moses. This is a homily on the two daughters and does not bear on the English.
Radak: the father of the people called Moab to this day. The English 'the father of the Moabites to this day' adopts this.

Ibn Ezra gives two readings of עַד הַיּוֹם: that no foreign nation mixed with them (the Moabites) up to now, or that the matter is known to this day. The English renders the words 'to this day' and decides neither reading; both are kept here.
Radak: 'from a father I had this son' (מֵאָב הָיָה לִי בֵּן זֶה): the meaning of the name מוֹאָב. The gloss and note give it; the English line keeps the name.

context: Moab was a people of the plateau east of the Dead Sea, a neighbour of Israel in the Transjordan. Deuteronomy 2:9 says that the LORD gave Ar to the descendants of Lot as a possession.
Moab is known also from outside the Bible: it is a kingdom in the Mesha stele, a royal inscription of Moab from the ninth century BCE.

The text gives Moab and Ammon an origin: both descend from Lot through his daughters, after the destruction of the cities (19:24-29). It states only the descent; whether the account preserves a tradition of kinship with these peoples or expresses Israel's view of them is discussed.

The name is explained by sound, as many names in Genesis are: 'Moab' is joined to מֵאָב, 'from a father'. Such explanations are the narrator's wordplay and are not necessarily the name's linguistic origin.

segments.english: And the younger also bore a son, and named him Ben-Ammi; he is the father of the Ammonites to this day.
segments.literal: and-the-younger also she bore son, and-named his-name Ben-Ammi, he father-of sons-of Ammon to the-day

tokens.note: The subject, the younger daughter, with the conjunction and the article on צָעִיר.
The emphatic pronoun resumes the subject: 'she also'.
Qatal of יָלַד, third feminine singular: a completed act in the narrative.
Wayyiqtol of קָרָא.

The name בֶּן־עַמִּי is a transliteration: 'son of my people' (the lexicon's gloss), or in Radak's words 'from my family'. It sounds like בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן, 'sons of Ammon', and the text links the two by sound. The English keeps the name, as the decisions require.
בְּנֵי, the sons of: the people as a whole, the descendants of the son.

phrases.literal: 'and-the-younger also': the subject, with the conjunction and the adverb
'she': the emphatic pronoun, resumed by the subject 'the younger'; the English does not repeat it
'bore son': the qatal, then the object
'and-named his-name Ben-Ammi': the idiom 'named him' for 'called his name'
'he father-of': a nominal clause with 'is' implicit
'sons-of Ammon': the people, as in 19:37
'to the-day': the fixed phrase

grammar: The verse repeats the frame of 19:37 with the younger daughter as subject. The emphatic pronoun גַם־הִוא is the one difference in the subject.
The name בֶּן־עַמִּי is the younger's naming of her son; its meaning ('son of my people') is in the note, not in the English line.
The Hebrew marks the end of a section after this verse (the ס in the Masoretic text), which closes the account of the two daughters.
בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן is a collective: 'the sons of Ammon' is the people, so the English gives 'the Ammonites'.

commentary.summary: Radak: the name בֶּן־עַמִּי means 'from my family I had this son'. And this daughter was more modest than the firstborn, for she did not reveal that he was from her father (שֶׁלֹּא גִּלְּתָה מִן אָבִיהָ).
Radak: the people is called the sons of Ammon, which is why the English gives 'the Ammonites' for the Hebrew phrase.

apparatus: The pronoun is written הוא and read הִיא (the Torah's regular ketiv/qere for the feminine pronoun); the pointing הִוא is the qere. The English follows the reading: 'she'.
context: Ammon was a people of the Transjordan, north-east of Moab and east of the Jordan, with its centre at Rabbah (later Amman). Deuteronomy 2:19 gives the land of the sons of Ammon to the descendants of Lot.
The name בֶּן־עַמִּי, 'son of my people', resembles בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן, 'sons of Ammon': as with Moab, the text joins the name of the people to the name of the child by sound.
